beliefs.practice: Read the DOCUMENTDB_URI from an environment variable at runtime; never commit it to source control. Provide a .env.example with a placeholder and document using an Azure Key Vault secret or other secrets store for production.

Use a singleton, shared Mongoose/MongoClient connection for the whole app instead of creating a new connection per request. Configure connection pool size (e.g., maxPoolSize), socketTimeoutMS and serverSelectionTimeoutMS in the connection options.
Require TLS/SSL for client connections and include tls=true (or tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=false) in the connection string; do not disable certificate validation in production.
Store monetary amounts using a precise numeric type (Decimal128 or integer smallest unit like cents). Do not use JavaScript Number (float) for currency values.

Enforce idempotency by creating a unique index on transactions.idempotencyKey (e.g., db.transactions.createIndex({idempotencyKey:1}, {unique:true, partialFilterExpression:{idempotencyKey:{$exists:true}}})). Use upsert/findOneAndUpdate with $setOnInsert or insert within a transaction and handle duplicate key errors gracefully.

Perform multi-document changes (posting a transaction plus any ledger state updates) inside a client session transaction (startSession + session.startTransaction + commitTransaction) and pass the session to all Mongoose operations involved.

Keep transactions short and small: touch as few documents as possible, avoid long-running work inside a transaction, and limit the size of documents modified in a single transaction to avoid memory/time limits.

Model exchange rates as documents keyed by currency pair and effective date, and index them for lookups: create a compound index {fromCurrency:1, toCurrency:1, effectiveDate:-1} so aggregation $lookup or application fetches get the latest rate quickly.

When converting amounts in aggregation pipelines, store and use a canonical rate direction (e.g., rate is amount of target per 1 source) and, if reverse lookup is needed, either store both directions or compute 1/rate in the pipeline; ensure Decimal128 propagation via $toDecimal where needed.

Avoid maintaining derived balances as eagerly-updated fields unless you can guarantee transactional updates and low contention; instead compute balances via aggregation over transactions or use carefully-provisioned atomic updates with optimistic concurrency.

Use compact, targeted aggregation pipelines: $match early, project only necessary fields, use indexes for $match/$sort, and set allowDiskUse:true for large groupings. Verify pipeline performance with explain() and use indexes to satisfy early $match stages.

Create an index on transactions.accountId and a compound index for common query patterns (e.g., {accountId:1, timestamp:-1, currency:1}) so balance and history queries are covered and avoid full-collection scans.

Make idempotency records compact and immutable (idempotencyKey, clientId, createdAt, responseRef). Use a TTL index if you only need idempotency for a bounded window (e.g., expire idempotency keys after configurable hours/days).

Implement retry with exponential backoff for transient network and server selection errors (MongoNetworkError, MongoServerSelectionError, retryable write errors). For non-idempotent operations use idempotency tokens or avoid automatic retry; for transactions, only retry entire transaction logic according to MongoDB transaction retry guidance (explicit retry loop with new session).

Use Decimal128, BigInt or integer minor-units everywhere conversion arithmetic is done in the app and avoid JavaScript floating-point arithmetic; run monetary arithmetic server-side in aggregation using $multiply/$divide with Decimal128 where possible.

Protect against duplicate inserts from concurrent clients by using findOneAndUpdate with upsert and $setOnInsert inside a transaction or rely on the unique index and catch duplicate key errors to return the existing result.

When using Mongoose with sessions, always pass {session} to all queries/updates and use session.withTransaction(callback) or explicit startTransaction/commitTransaction to ensure operations are part of the same transaction.

Monitor indexes with explain() and the cluster tools to ensure aggregation stages use the expected index; create covered indexes for heavy read paths and avoid over-indexing write-hot collections to reduce write amplification and RU costs.
Limit document size (MongoDB document limit ~16MB) and design transactions so they don't accumulate large in-memory operations; paginate large result sets and use streaming/cursors for large exports.

If leveraging vector capabilities (embeddings) do not index high-dimensional vectors with B-tree indexes; use the cluster’s vector index types (HNSW/IVF) with appropriate dimension, metric (cosine/inner), and index parameters (efConstruction, M or nlist) and control query 'ef'/'probe' for recall/latency tradeoffs.
